rationale: Extended the healed-partition case so the path the account recorded as unexercised is now measured: after the connections are restored and one client entry is driven into whichever instance leads, the case compares the two sides' stores for the first index at which they disagree, reads both sides' applied positions, and searches each instance's FSM for the payloads. Construction-time local feedback with the flag enabled: the two stores still disagreed at log index 118, where the first side held a LogConfiguration entry and the second side a LogCommand entry (the first side's payload at 119, the second side's at 118), yet both sides had applied through index 121 - the first side's applied position 121 and the minimum applied position of the two peers 121 - and the post-heal client entry committed at 121 and was applied by the restarted instance and by both peers, so the cluster kept committing to every instance while two of its state machines held different applied values for log index 118. With the flag disabled the same measurement reported no disagreeing index, applied positions of 119 on both sides and one committed entry. This is the state-machine-level form of the divergence the account recorded only in log stores, and it addresses the speculation that a later election or replication could reconcile the two sides: continued client traffic replicated over the conflict without touching it.

experiment.revision_reason: Adds an applied-state phase to the healed partition: after healing, one client entry is driven into whichever instance leads, then the first index at which the two sides' stores disagree, both sides' applied positions, and each instance's FSM contents for the two divergent payloads and the new payload are reported, so whether two state machines hold different applied values for the same log index is observed instead of inferred. Comparison set replaced with the two previously recorded healed predicates, their control, the new applied-divergence predicate and its control, and the continuation predicate.

scope.description: What the healed partition leaves in the two sides' applied state when the cluster keeps serving clients. The predecessor's twenty-one cases are unchanged and the split_configurations case is extended a second time: after the two sides are reconnected and the leader count and surviving entries are reported, whichever instance is in Leader state receives one client entry with a 1500 ms timeout, the case waits its election window, then compares the restarted instance's store with the first peer's store for the lowest index at which the two hold entries that differ, reads both sides' last log index and applied position, and searches each instance's FSM for the two divergent payloads and the new payload.
assumptions: Real raft instances in one process over the in-memory transports and the in-memory commit-tracking log store from the captured package; healing uses the transport's own Connect in both directions and no instance is restarted, reconfigured or removed afterwards.

Each instance applies the entries its own log store holds between its applied position and the index it has been told is committed, so an instance whose applied position has reached an index has applied whatever entry its own store holds there.

The two divergent entries were committed on their own sides before healing, as recorded by the split_result event of the same run, and the first peer's store is compared because both peers of the committed configuration hold the second side's entry.

The disagreement index is taken over the range the two stores share and reports both entry types there, so a difference in committed content at one index is separated from one store simply holding more entries.
The FSM search uses the same exact payload strings, and the new payload is a fresh unique string applied after healing.
excluded: Disk-backed stores, real networks, membership reconciliation by an operator, entries applied through a snapshot transfer, and any claim about how long the divergence persists beyond the observed window.

experiment.prefix: The case is the predecessor's: three peers with MakeClusterCustom(MakeClusterOpts{Peers: 3, Bootstrap: true, CommitTrackingLogs: true, Conf: inmemConfig with TrailingLogs 10 and RestoreCommittedLogs set per case}), both non-leader peers demoted, 100 commands, leader.Snapshot(), both peers promoted and ten more entries applied, the leader disconnected from both peers in both directions and shut down, only it restarted over its own stores with the case flag beside one fresh empty instance, both sides allowed to elect and to commit uniquely named entries, and split_result and split_healed CA_EVENTs emitted as before. The case now additionally looks for an instance in Leader state, applies one uniquely named post-heal payload there with a 1500 ms timeout and records whether it committed and at which index, waits 800 ms, then calls probeFirstDivergence over the restarted instance's store and the first peer's store - the lowest index in the shared range at which type, term or data differ, with both entry types - and reads both stores' LastIndex and both sides' applied position, taking the minimum of the two peers' positions. It searches the restarted instance's FSM and both peers' FSMs for the two divergent payloads and for the post-heal payload, and emits one applied_state CA_EVENT with the disagreement index and the two entry types there, both sides' last index and applied position, both payload indices and whether they coincide, whether the first side's FSM applied its own divergent payload, the post-heal commit outcome and index, how many FSMs on each side applied it, the derived divergent_applied_same_index field, and the wait.
experiment.responsibility: A node applies the entries its own log store holds between its applied position and the index it knows to be committed, so two nodes whose stores hold different committed entries at one index keep two different applied values for that index once both have applied past it, and ordinary replication after healing leaves that untouched because the two entries agree in the term that the index-and-term comparison uses.

comparisons.description: Healing with the flag enabled: after the connections are restored the cluster is expected to converge on a single leader.
Healing with the flag enabled: only one of the two divergent committed entries is expected to remain in the cluster once it has converged.

Healing with the flag enabled, after further client traffic: no two instances are expected to have applied different committed values for the same log index, which the case reports when the two stores still disagree at an index both sides have applied past.

Healing with the flag enabled: a client entry applied after healing is expected to reach the FSM of every instance of the committed configuration, so two applied values for one index is not an artefact of a stalled cluster.
Control: with the flag disabled the two sides never split, so their stores agree over the shared range and no index is reported as holding two different applied values.
Control: with the flag disabled only the single committed entry exists, so exactly one survives healing trivially.
